passages.t: For the sake of God's name
passages.happening:
In the seventh year, some elders come to inquire of the LORD. God refuses: ‘As surely as I live, I will not be consulted by you’ (verse 3). Instead Ezekiel is to confront them with the history of their fathers (verse 4).

When God chose Israel in Egypt, he told them to throw away the idols of Egypt, but they rebelled. ‘But I acted for the sake of My name, that it should not be profaned in the eyes of the nations’ (verse 9), and he brought them out. In the wilderness he gave them his statutes, ‘for the man who does these things will live by them’ (verse 11), and his Sabbaths ‘as a sign between us’ (verse 12). They rebelled again, and again God held back for the sake of his name (verses 13-17). Their children did the same (verses 18-24). So God says, ‘I also gave them over to statutes that were not good and ordinances by which they could not live’ (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The date is the summer of 591 BC, about five years before Jerusalem fell. The elders came hoping for a word of quick return. For God to refuse to be consulted was itself a verdict.

The history is retold as a pattern: rebellion, deserved judgment, and mercy for the sake of God's name. The oath with an uplifted hand pictures someone swearing a solemn vow. For exiles far from the temple, with no altar, keeping the Sabbath was one of the few public marks of belonging to the LORD, which is why it weighs so heavily here.
passages.later: God calls the Sabbath ‘a sign between Me and you for the generations to come’ (Exodus 31:13). A psalm says, ‘So I gave them up to their stubborn hearts’ (Psalm 81:12).
passages.hard:
What does God mean when he says he gave Israel statutes that were not good (verses 25-26)?

These verses are among the hardest in the prophets, because they seem to say that God gave laws that led to death, even to the sacrifice of children. Interpreters offer several readings. Many read them as a judicial handing over: because Israel rejected God's good laws, he gave them up to the destructive practices they preferred, as the psalm says God gave his people up to their stubborn hearts. The BSB's wording, gave them over, reflects this reading. Others think Ezekiel refers to Israel's twisted reading of a real law, the command to give the firstborn to the LORD, which the law says must be redeemed for sons, but which some turned into child sacrifice. Ezekiel would then be quoting their claim that God demanded it, a claim Jeremiah flatly denies.

Every reading agrees that the chapter condemns the sacrifice of children as the height of defilement and never presents it as something God desired.
passages.asks: Again and again God held back his judgment for the sake of his name. Ask what it means that his faithfulness does not depend on yours. And ask where you need to stop testing his patience.

passages.t: A new exodus, and acceptance on the holy mountain
passages.happening:
In the land, the fathers worshiped on every high hill, and the present generation does the same (verses 27-31). Now the exiles say, ‘Let us be like the nations, like the peoples of the lands, serving wood and stone’ (verse 32). God says it will never happen. ‘With a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and outpoured wrath I will rule over you’ (verse 33). He will bring them ‘into the wilderness of the nations’ and judge them face to face, as he judged their fathers in the wilderness of Egypt, and purge the rebels (verses 35-38).

Then, ‘on My holy mountain, the high mountain of Israel’, the whole house of Israel will serve him, and he will accept them ‘as a pleasing aroma’ (verses 40-41). They will remember their ways and loathe themselves, and know that he has dealt with them ‘for the sake of My name and not according to your wicked ways’ (verse 44). A short word about fire in the forest of the south follows, and Ezekiel complains that people say he only tells parables (verses 45-49).
passages.hearers:
Verse 32 voices a real temptation of exile: to settle down and serve the gods of the land where you now live, like every other displaced people. God refuses to let his people dissolve into the nations.

The new exodus mirrors the old one. As Israel once passed through the wilderness between Egypt and the land, so the exiles will pass through a wilderness of judgment before they are restored. The strong hand and outstretched arm are the words of the exodus from Egypt.

In Hebrew Bibles, verses 45 to 49 begin chapter 21.
passages.later: God promised at the exodus, ‘I will redeem you with an outstretched arm’ (Exodus 6:6). Hosea heard that God would lead Israel into the wilderness and speak tenderly to her (Hosea 2:14).
passages.asks: The exiles were tempted to blend in and become like everyone around them. Ask where you feel that pull most. And ask what it means that God will not let his people go.
